t: Sum of K Subarrays With Length at Least M — Suffix DP
o: Pick k disjoint subarrays, each of length >= m, maximizing total sum; elements can be negative. With n <= 2000, an O(n*k) DP fits comfortably. Example 1: two subarrays [1,2] and [3,3,4] give 13. Example 2 forces taking every element as its own subarray, totaling -10. The guarantee k <= n/m ensures a valid selection always exists.
k: Define dp[i][k] = best answer using suffix starting at index i with k subarrays remaining.
A subarray starting at i has length >= m; handle arbitrary lengths via a helper state that extends the current subarray one element at a time.
Recurrence: dp[i][k] = max(dp[i+1][k], nums[i] + ext[i+1][k]) where ext[i][k] = max(sum(i..i+m-1)+dp[i+m][k-1], nums[i]+ext[i+1][k]).

a.i: dp[i][k]: best using nums[i..] with k subarrays left — either skip index i, or start a subarray here. Starting a subarray of length >= m is captured by ext[i][k]: either fix its first m elements then recurse, or include nums[i] and keep extending. This avoids enumerating all lengths explicitly.
s: Compute suffix-free dp table bottom-up from i = n down to 0.
a.t: O(n*k) — each (index, subarrays-left) pair is computed once with O(1) work.
a.sp: O(n*k) for the two DP tables.

w: The two-state trick (start vs. extend) is the key insight; without it, naive length enumeration gives O(n^2 k). Pitfalls: off-by-one on prefix sums, needing 64-bit sums (values up to 10^4 * 2000), and initializing ext to -infinity while dp defaults to 0. Follow-ups: reconstruct the actual subarrays (store parent pointers), or handle larger m with the same recurrence (still O(nk)).
